common_name: Inca Plum (Heart-Shaped Golden Heirloom Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Inca is a long-grown Southern heirloom Japanese plum needing only about 250 chill hours, so it sets a reliable crop through most Gulf South winters.

directions: Inca has been grown in home orchards across the South since the early twentieth century and remains valued for its distinctive heart-shaped, golden-skinned fruit marked with magenta speckling and a rosy blush near the stem. Its roughly 250-hour chill requirement is low enough to satisfy most Gulf Coast zone 8-9 winters, and the flesh is dense, crisp, and notably tart-sweet compared to softer modern Japanese plums. Plant a second compatible Japanese plum cultivar, such as Methley or Morris, nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune annually in late winter to an open center to improve airflow and reduce the bacterial and fungal disease pressure common in humid Southern summers.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension (Harris County) — Recommended Fruit and Nut Varieties
Aggie Horticulture — Recommended Fruit and Nut Varieties

common_name: Robusto Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Vigorous Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Robusto is a vigorous, upright USDA-ARS Byron, Georgia release with a chill requirement in the 400-500 hour range, suited to the cooler pockets of the Gulf South.

directions: Robusto came out of the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program in Byron, Georgia, the same research station behind Byrongold and Ruby Sweet, and produces a tall, upright, semi-spreading tree that bears heavily. Fruit is red-skinned with yellow flesh and ripens early, in late May to early June, ahead of most other Southeastern plums. Its chill requirement runs 400-500 hours, higher than the true ultra-low-chill Gulf series plums, so it performs best in interior zone 8 orchards rather than the mildest coastal fringe. It is not reliably self-fruitful, so plant it with a second compatible Japanese plum, such as Morris or Methley, for cross-pollination and consistent fruit set.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, Georgia Stone Fruit Breeding Program
University of Florida IFAS — Growing Plums in Florida (HS250)

common_name: Segundo Plum (USDA Georgia-Bred Red-Skinned Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Segundo is a USDA-ARS Byron, Georgia release with a chill requirement of roughly 400-500 hours, making it best suited to the cooler interior parts of the Gulf South rather than the mildest coastal zones.

directions: Segundo was developed by the USDA-ARS stone fruit breeding program in Byron, Georgia, the same station that produced Byrongold and Ruby Sweet, and bears red-skinned, yellow-fleshed fruit that ripens mid-to-late June, somewhat later than earlier Gulf-series selections. The fruit is soft-textured and best used fresh shortly after harvest rather than stored. Its chill requirement of roughly 400-500 hours places it toward the upper end of what the Gulf South can reliably deliver, so it is best reserved for zone 8 gardens with fuller winter chill rather than the warmest coastal zone 9 sites. Plant a second compatible Japanese plum cultivar nearby, since Segundo is not dependably self-fruitful.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, Georgia Stone Fruit Breeding Program
Journal of the American Pomological Society — 'Segundo,' 'Byrongold' and 'Rubysweet' Plums and BY69-1637P Plumcot
